clue.text: World poem rewrite for 16 creation

indicators.note: to rewrite a text is to recast it, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

parts.note: these two words are the anagram fodder, as corrected for the setter's slip recorded with this clue

explanation.surface: A request to recast a poem about the world for some other entry's purposes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrite' shuffles WORLD POEM, but those nine letters lack the I of the answer; the setter (or the print) dropped one letter. 16 across is POWELL, the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Widmerpool is the famous grasping character in Anthony Powell's novel sequence A Dance to the Music of Time.

clue.text: Reckless character of England's Fielding

explanation.surface: A description of a rash figure from Henry Fielding's fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild means rash and uncontrolled; Jonathan Wild is the criminal hero of Henry Fielding's satirical novel.

clue.text: Pastoral poet uses cart with heavy load

parts.note: a dray is a low heavy cart, such as a brewer's
a ton is a large weight, used loosely of any heavy burden

explanation.surface: A poet of the countryside travels by laden farm cart.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Drayton, the Elizabethan writer, composed pastorals such as Idea, the Shepherd's Garland.

clue.text: Spenserian song adapted by Gustafson in wartime

explanation.surface: A Renaissance wedding song reworked by a modern poet during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: Ralph Gustafson, a Canadian poet, wrote 'Epithalamium in Time of War' (1941), adapting Spenser's form.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser wrote a marriage ode by this title for his own wedding, and Gustafson's wartime poem borrows its form and name.

clue.text: Composer indicates heathen in one

parts.note: a pagan is a heathen, someone outside the main religions
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A musician hints that an unbeliever is among us.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolò Paganini, the Italian violin virtuoso, also wrote music, including his famous caprices.

clue.text: Preferred to lemon with fish by Carol Shields

explanation.surface: A choice of citrus over lemon to go with fish, made by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol Shields published a story collection called The Orange Fish (1989).
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit is chosen in place of a lemon, and the colour word names Shields's fish in her collection's title.

clue.text: Goddess from the other Athenian pantheon

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, so 'from' signals a buried word

explanation.surface: A deity drawn from the gods worshipped by some other Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Hera is the queen of the Olympian deities, wife of Zeus.

clue.text: University on continent briefly reveals Gorgon

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece standing on another comes after it

parts.note: EUR is the short form of Europe
Yale is the American Ivy League university

explanation.surface: A trip to a European college turns up a mythical monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Euryale is one of the three snake-haired sisters of Greek myth, alongside Stheno and Medusa.

clue.text: Uncontrolled carnal glee shown by hypocrite with murderous wife

indicators.note: glee that is uncontrolled runs wild, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Wild sensual pleasure displayed by a two-faced man whose wife kills.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Angel Clare rejects Tess for a past like his own; she later kills Alec.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Angel Clare condemns Tess for the very fault he confesses himself, and Tess goes on to commit murder.

clue.text: Top of the bill in Magdalen, perhaps

indicators.note: here 'perhaps' says the words may be arranged another way, so their letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: Who heads the playbill at an Oxford college show.
explanation.walkthrough: Magdalen is an Oxford college, which makes the surface sound like a student production.
explanation.definitionFit: A leading man is the principal male actor, the star whose name is billed first.

clue.text: Clasped by Tennyson's eagle

parts.note: Tennyson's short poem The Eagle opens with the bird clasping a rock face with crooked hands

explanation.definitionFit: The poem's first line has the eagle gripping a steep rocky height high above the sea.

clue.text: An especially venomous Sayers offering

parts.note: a very toxic substance given by a crime writer, also the title of one of her Wimsey novels

explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy L. Sayers wrote a 1930 detective novel by this title, in which Harriet Vane is tried for arsenic murder.

clue.text: "Most people have a furious — to talk about themselves" (Somerset Maugham)

definitions.text: "Most people have a furious — to talk about themselves" (Somerset Maugham)

parts.words: "Most people have a furious — to talk about themselves" (Somerset Maugham)
parts.note: the missing word in Maugham's remark is a craving or urge

explanation.definitionFit: Maugham's line uses the word for a restless desire, as an urge one cannot ignore.

clue.text: Auden said that birds turn their head at her approach

definitions.text: Auden said that birds turn their head at her approach

parts.words: Auden said that birds turn their head at her approach
parts.note: Auden's verse for a 1936 documentary film describes a train passing at night, birds turning their heads

explanation.definitionFit: Auden's poem for the GPO film follows the overnight postal train from London to Scotland.

clue.text: Izaak does not start at gated section of river, we are told, in Kingsley's work

indicators.note: a name that does not start loses its first letter, here from the angler's surname

parts.note: Izaak Walton wrote The Compleat Angler

indicators.note: what we are told is heard spoken, so the word sounds like the one entered

parts.note: a lock is a stretch of river closed by gates to raise or lower boats

explanation.surface: An angler arrives late at a river lock in a Victorian novelist's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley's 1850 novel follows a Chartist tailor-poet of that name.

clue.text: Early poet from German director's territory

parts.note: Fritz Lang was the German film director of Metropolis
land is territory

explanation.surface: A medieval poet hails from a film-maker's homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: William Langland, author of Piers Plowman, wrote in the fourteenth century.

clue.text: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing

definitions.text: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing

parts.words: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing
parts.note: the novelist whose twelve-volume sequence opens with the book A Question of Upbringing

explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell began A Dance to the Music of Time with A Question of Upbringing in 1951.

clue.text: Prohibition at French town for prominent Irish writer

parts.note: a ban is a prohibition
ville is French for town

explanation.surface: A ban imposed in a French town on a famous Irish author.
explanation.definitionFit: John Banville is a Booker-winning Irish novelist, author of The Sea.

clue.text: Giant and some overactors present old characters

parts.note: Og, king of Bashan, is a giant in the Bible
hams are actors who overact

explanation.surface: A huge figure and several hammy actors put on a show of ancient roles.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is an early Irish alphabet, so its letters are ancient written symbols.

clue.text: Novel sort of rogue

parts.note: a fiction title in which the surname follows the word rogue

explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Walpole's 1930 novel Rogue Herries makes the family name a particular kind of rogue.

clue.text: Josephine Tay's was Time's

parts.note: Josephine Tey's 1951 detective novel is named for a child of Time

explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints the novelist's name as 'Tay'; she is Josephine Tey.
explanation.definitionFit: Tey's novel The Daughter of Time takes its title from the proverb that truth is Time's child.

clue.text: Loftier form of Benson work

indicators.note: a form of a word is a version of it, so its letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A grander version of a book by Benson.
explanation.definitionFit: A.C. Benson wrote The Trefoil, a memoir of three places he knew: Wellington College, Lincoln and Truro.

clue.text: Goddess in heathen attachment

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the two words that follow, running across the gap

explanation.surface: A deity whom pagans are devoted to.
explanation.definitionFit: Athena is the Greek deity of wisdom and war, patron of Athens.

clue.text: No, I'm not Byron (—)

parts.note: the dash asks for the author of a Russian lyric that begins with these words

explanation.definitionFit: Mikhail Lermontov wrote the 1832 poem 'No, I am not Byron, I am another'.

clue.text: Writer on love is frank

indicators.note: one piece put on another follows it here

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
a pen is a writing implement

explanation.surface: An author who writes about love is candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Open describes speech that is honest and candid, hiding nothing.

clue.text: "When the past has latched its postern behind my tremulous —" (Thomas Hardy)

definitions.text: "When the past has latched its postern behind my tremulous —" (Thomas Hardy)

parts.words: "When the past has latched its postern behind my tremulous —" (Thomas Hardy)
parts.note: the missing word in Hardy's poem Afterwards means a period of remaining

explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Afterwards opens with his lifetime as a sojourn, a brief period of remaining.

clue.text: Historic inspiration with cooking oil at start of century

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
cooking a figure or a book means fiddling it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Inspiration from the past, with a splash of cooking oil at the turn of the century.
explanation.definitionFit: Clio is the Muse of history in Greek myth, the one who inspires historians.

clue.text: Underworld second sight not inaccurately recalling old straits

parts.note: hell is the underworld
ESP, extrasensory perception, is second sight

indicators.note: a word set down inaccurately has its letters out of place, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: A vision of the underworld recalls an ancient sea passage, accurately enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not inaccurately' reads as 'quite correctly', but 'inaccurately' shuffles the word 'not' to ONT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hellespont is the ancient name for the Dardanelles strait, crossed by Leander.

clue.text: Direction taken by Rugby

explanation.surface: The way a famous school went.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is the English public school of Tom Brown's Schooldays, where Harry East is Tom's friend.
explanation.definitionFit: One compass point, and the surname of Tom Brown's schoolfellow at Rugby.

clue.text: Way of viewing subjects of Gorky, Phillpotts, Buck and Benson

definitions.text: Way of viewing subjects of Gorky, Phillpotts, Buck and Benson

parts.words: Way of viewing subjects of Gorky, Phillpotts, Buck and Benson
parts.note: each of these writers produced a book titled Mother or The Mother, so the outlook is a parent's

explanation.definitionFit: Gorky, Pearl Buck and others wrote novels about a mother, and viewing as she does is the adverb for a mother's manner.
